questions.stem:
(a) Write notes on each of the following:
(i) Great Circles;
(ii) Local Time.
(b) A concert arranged to commence at 12 midnight on Sunday in Sydney (Australia) 150 degrees E is to be televised. When will a family wishing to watch the programme in Accra (Ghana) tune in to the television for the programme?
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) A great circle is a circle on the earth's surface whose plane passes through the centre of the earth, dividing it into two equal hemispheres
2 marks: (a)(i) Examples: the equator and any pair of opposite meridians; the shortest distance between two points lies along a great circle, so it is used by ships and aircraft
2 marks: (a)(ii) Local time is the time at a place determined by the position of the sun; it is 12 noon when the sun is overhead at that meridian
2 marks: (a)(ii) The earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, i.e. 15 degrees per hour or 1 degree per 4 minutes; places east gain time, places west lose time
2 marks: (b) Accra is about 0 degrees; difference in longitude = 150 - 0 = 150 degrees
2 marks: (b) Time difference = 150 / 15 = 10 hours
2 marks: (b) Accra is west of Sydney, so its time is 10 hours behind: 12 midnight - 10 hours
2 marks: (b) The family should tune in at 2.00 p.m. on Sunday
questions.explanation: (a)(i) A great circle is any circle on the globe whose plane passes through the earth's centre, so that it divides the earth into two equal halves. The equator is the only parallel that is a great circle, while every meridian with its opposite meridian forms one. An arc of a great circle is the shortest route between two places, so great circle routes are used in air and sea navigation. (ii) Local time is the time of a place reckoned by the sun: it is noon when the sun is highest over that meridian. Because the earth rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours, time changes by 1 hour for every 15 degrees (4 minutes per degree) of longitude, places to the east being ahead and those to the west behind. (b) Accra lies about 0 degrees, so the longitude difference with Sydney is 150 degrees, giving 150 / 15 = 10 hours. Accra is west, so it is 10 hours behind: midnight on Sunday in Sydney is 2.00 p.m. on Sunday in Accra.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the three classes of sedimentary rocks.
(b) Explain with examples, the processes of formation of the three classes of sedimentary rocks.
(c) State four uses of rocks to man.
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Mechanically formed, organically formed and chemically formed sedimentary rocks
3 marks: (b) Mechanically formed: weathered rock fragments are transported by rivers, wind, ice or waves, deposited in layers, compacted and cemented, e.g. sandstone, shale, clay, conglomerate
3 marks: (b) Organically formed: remains of plants and animals accumulate and are compressed, e.g. coal/lignite from plants, limestone/chalk/coral from shells and skeletons
3 marks: (b) Chemically formed: minerals precipitate from solution when water evaporates or by chemical reaction, e.g. rock salt, gypsum, potash, trona
4 marks: (c) Building and construction materials (stone, gravel, cement from limestone); sources of minerals and fuels (coal, petroleum); soil formation for agriculture; tourism/scenery; making glass, ceramics and fertilisers (any four, 1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) Sedimentary rocks are mechanically formed, organically formed and chemically formed. (b) Mechanically formed rocks develop when fragments of older rocks produced by weathering are carried by rivers, wind, ice or waves and deposited in layers, which are then compressed and cemented; examples are sandstone, shale, clay and conglomerate. Organically formed rocks come from the accumulated remains of living things: plant matter buried and compressed becomes peat, lignite and coal, while shells and skeletons of marine organisms form limestone, chalk and coral. Chemically formed rocks result from precipitation of dissolved minerals, for example when water in lakes or lagoons evaporates, leaving rock salt, gypsum, potash or trona. (c) Rocks provide building materials (stones, gravel, limestone for cement), contain minerals and fuels such as coal and petroleum, weather into soil for agriculture, and attract tourists with their scenery; some are raw materials for glass and ceramics.

questions.stem:
The table below shows the climatic data of a station in the world.
Month: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, June, July, Aug, Sept, Oct, Nov, Dec.
Temp in degrees C: 23, 24, 29, 32, 31, 37, 27, 26, 27, 27, 26, 27.
Rainfall in mm: 0, 2, 2, 13, 64, 122, 208, 300, 140, 13, 0, 0.
Use the data provided to answer the following questions:
(a)(i) Calculate the temperature range.
(ii) Find the annual rainfall for the station.
(iii) State the hemisphere in which the station can be found.
(iv) Suggest the climatic type.
(v) Give one reason for your suggestion.
(b)(i) Indicate the type of vegetation associated with the climate suggested in a(iv) above.
(ii) Explain three characteristic features of the vegetation that have enabled it to adapt to the type of climate mentioned above.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Range = 37 - 23 = 14 degrees C
2 marks: (a)(ii) Annual rainfall = 864 mm
1 mark: (a)(iii) Northern hemisphere (rain and highest temperatures between April and September)
2 marks: (a)(iv) Tropical continental (Sudan savanna) climate
2 marks: (a)(v) High temperatures all year with a single rainy season (May-September, peak in August) and a long dry season of about 5-7 months; moderate total rainfall
1 mark: (b)(i) Savanna (tropical grassland with scattered trees)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Trees have long tap roots to reach underground water during the dry season
2 marks: (b)(ii) Trees are deciduous/have small or waxy leaves to reduce transpiration; grasses dry up and lie dormant in the dry season
2 marks: (b)(ii) Thick, fire-resistant bark (and water-storing trunks, e.g. baobab) to survive bush fires and drought
questions.explanation: (a)(i) The highest temperature is 37 degrees C (June) and the lowest 23 degrees C (January), so the range is 14 degrees C. (ii) Adding the monthly rainfall: 0 + 2 + 2 + 13 + 64 + 122 + 208 + 300 + 140 + 13 + 0 + 0 = 864 mm. (iii) The rain and hottest months fall between April and September, so the station is in the northern hemisphere. (iv) It has a tropical continental (Sudan savanna) climate, (v) because temperatures are high throughout the year and rainfall is concentrated in one season of about five months, with a long dry season of nearly no rain from October to March. (b)(i) The associated vegetation is savanna, tall grasses with scattered trees. (ii) The trees have long tap roots that reach deep groundwater during the dry season; they are deciduous or have small, thick or waxy leaves to reduce water loss, while grasses wither and remain dormant until the rains; and they have thick, fire-resistant bark, some like the baobab storing water in their swollen trunks.

questions.stem:
Study the pie-chart (Figure 1) showing the components of a mature soil, and answer the following questions. [The pie-chart shows four sectors: weathered parent rock (about half of the circle), water, organic matter, and a fourth sector marked '?'.]
(a) Identify
(i) the fourth component.
(ii) two contributions of the fourth component to the soil formation.
(b) Describe
(i) how the organic material is derived.
(ii) the difference between a peat-soil and a mature soil.
(c) Explain three ways by which a soil that is eroded can be improved for farming.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Air (soil air)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Supplies oxygen for respiration of soil organisms and plant roots, aiding decomposition of organic matter; supplies nitrogen for nitrogen-fixing bacteria and aids chemical weathering (oxidation)
3 marks: (b)(i) Organic matter is derived from the remains of dead plants and animals and animal wastes, decomposed by bacteria, fungi and other organisms into humus
3 marks: (b)(ii) Peat soil is formed in waterlogged, poorly aerated areas and consists mainly of partly decomposed plant material (very high organic content, acidic); a mature soil has well-developed horizons with balanced mineral matter, humus, water and air
2 marks: (c) Adding organic manure/compost or fertilisers to restore lost nutrients
2 marks: (c) Planting cover crops/grasses and practising crop rotation and fallowing
2 marks: (c) Contour ploughing, terracing, mulching or building ridges/bunds across slopes to check further erosion
questions.explanation: (a)(i) The fourth component is air. (ii) Soil air supplies oxygen for the respiration of roots and soil organisms such as bacteria and earthworms that decompose organic matter into humus, supplies nitrogen used by nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and helps chemical weathering through oxidation of the parent material. (b)(i) Organic matter comes from dead leaves, stems, roots and animal remains and droppings, which are broken down by bacteria, fungi and other soil organisms to form humus. (ii) Peat soil forms in waterlogged, poorly aerated places where decomposition is slow, so it consists mostly of partly decayed plant matter, is dark and acidic and has little mineral matter; a mature soil has distinct horizons and a balanced mixture of weathered mineral particles, humus, water and air. (c) Eroded soil can be improved by adding manure, compost or fertilisers to replace lost nutrients; by planting cover crops, rotating crops and allowing fallow periods to rebuild organic matter and protect the surface; and by contour ploughing, terracing, mulching or building ridges and bunds to slow run-off and prevent further loss.

questions.stem:
(b) Account for the occurrence of
(i) Low Pressure belt along the equator.
(ii) Sub-Tropical High Pressure belts.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (b)(i) The sun is overhead at or near the equator throughout the year, so temperatures are high
2 marks: (b)(i) Heated air expands, becomes light and rises by convection, creating low pressure (the doldrums/equatorial low)
1 mark: (b)(i) Converging trade winds and high humidity (moist air is lighter) add to the rising air
2 marks: (b)(ii) Air rising at the equator cools, spreads polewards in the upper atmosphere and, deflected by the earth's rotation, accumulates about 30 degrees N and S
2 marks: (b)(ii) The cool, dense air descends (subsides) there, increasing surface pressure
1 mark: (b)(ii) Descending air warms adiabatically and is dry, giving the high pressure belts (horse latitudes) and deserts
questions.explanation: (i) At the equator the sun is overhead or nearly so throughout the year, so the surface and the air above it are strongly heated. The warm, moist air expands, becomes lighter and rises in strong convection currents, and the trade winds converge to replace it, producing a belt of low pressure called the doldrums. (ii) The air that rises at the equator cools and moves polewards at high levels; deflected by the earth's rotation (Coriolis force), it piles up at about 30 to 35 degrees north and south. This cooled, dense air sinks towards the surface, raising pressure, and as it descends it is warmed and dried, creating the sub-tropical high pressure belts (horse latitudes) associated with the hot deserts.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between an ecosystem and a food chain.
(b) Explain the various ways man has affected the ecosystem.
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) An ecosystem is a natural unit consisting of all living organisms (plants, animals, micro-organisms) in an area interacting with one another and with their non-living environment (soil, water, air, climate)
3 marks: (a) A food chain is a linear sequence of organisms through which energy and nutrients pass as one organism eats another, e.g. grass - grasshopper - lizard - hawk; it is only part of an ecosystem
2 marks: (b) Deforestation/lumbering and clearing for farming destroy habitats and reduce biodiversity
2 marks: (b) Pollution of air, water and land by industries, oil spills, chemicals and refuse
2 marks: (b) Bush burning, overgrazing and poor farming practices cause soil erosion and desertification
2 marks: (b) Mining and urbanisation/construction of roads and dams alter landscapes and drainage
2 marks: (b) Positive effects: afforestation, conservation, game reserves and irrigation improve ecosystems
questions.explanation: (a) An ecosystem is a community of living organisms (plants, animals and decomposers) interacting with each other and with the non-living components of their environment such as soil, water, air and climate, e.g. a pond or a forest. A food chain is a single linear feeding sequence by which energy passes from producers through a series of consumers, e.g. grass to grasshopper to lizard to hawk; it is one part of the energy flow within an ecosystem. (b) Man has affected ecosystems by clearing forests for timber, farming and settlements, destroying habitats and species; by polluting air, water and land with industrial wastes, oil spills, agro-chemicals and refuse; by bush burning, overgrazing and poor farming, which lead to soil erosion and desert encroachment; and by mining, urbanisation and building dams and roads, which change landforms and drainage. Man has also improved ecosystems through afforestation, conservation, game reserves and irrigation.

questions.stem:
(a) Define the term soil erosion.
(b) Explain the various physical factors which can encourage soil erosion.
(c) Outline four ways of preventing coastal erosion.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Soil erosion is the removal/wearing away of the top soil by agents such as running water, wind and waves faster than it can be formed
2 marks: (b) Heavy, intense rainfall (tropical rainstorms) produces much run-off that washes away soil
2 marks: (b) Steep slopes increase the speed of run-off
2 marks: (b) Lack of vegetation cover leaves soil exposed; strong winds in dry areas blow away loose soil
2 marks: (b) Nature of the soil: loose, sandy or poorly structured soils with little humus are easily eroded
2 marks: (c) Building sea walls, groynes and breakwaters
2 marks: (c) Planting vegetation (e.g. mangroves, grasses) on beaches and dunes; beach nourishment/dumping sand and rocks (rip-rap) along the shore
2 marks: (c) Controlling sand mining and construction near the shore; enforcing coastal management laws
questions.explanation: (a) Soil erosion is the removal of the top layer of soil by agents such as running water, wind and waves at a rate faster than new soil is formed. (b) Physical factors that encourage it include heavy and intense tropical rainfall, which produces large amounts of run-off; steep slopes, which speed up the flow of water; lack of vegetation cover, leaving the soil unprotected from raindrops and strong winds; and the nature of the soil, since loose, sandy soils with little organic matter are easily detached. (c) Coastal erosion can be prevented by building sea walls, groynes and breakwaters; by planting mangroves and grasses to stabilise beaches and dunes; by replenishing beaches with sand or placing boulders (rip-rap) along the shore; and by banning sand mining near the shore and enforcing coastal zone regulations.

questions.stem:
(a) Account for the rapid population growth in the developing world.
(b) Identify three problems associated with the rapid population growth.
(c) Suggest any four possible remedies for these problems.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) High birth rates due to early marriage and polygamy
2 marks: (a) Falling death rates due to improved medical care, vaccination and sanitation
2 marks: (a) Cultural/religious beliefs favouring large families and low use of family planning; children seen as source of labour and security in old age
2 marks: (a) Illiteracy/low education of women and improved food supply
2 marks: (b) Unemployment and underemployment
2 marks: (b) Pressure on social amenities (schools, hospitals, housing, water) and growth of slums
2 marks: (b) Food shortages, poverty and increased crime/environmental degradation
1 mark: (c) Family planning and population education
1 mark: (c) Industrialisation and job creation
2 marks: (c) Mechanised agriculture to increase food supply
2 marks: (c) Provision of more social amenities; education of women and discouraging early marriage
questions.explanation: (a) Population is growing rapidly in developing countries because birth rates remain high, encouraged by early marriage, polygamy, religious and cultural preference for large families, the need for children as farm labour and old-age security, and limited use of family planning, especially among illiterate women. At the same time death rates have fallen sharply thanks to better medical care, vaccination, sanitation and food supply, so natural increase is high. (b) The problems include unemployment and underemployment; overstretched social amenities such as schools, hospitals, housing and water supply, with the growth of slums; and food shortages, poverty, rising crime and environmental degradation. (c) Remedies include family planning and population education; industrialisation to create jobs; mechanisation of agriculture to increase food production; and provision of more social amenities, together with education of women and discouragement of early marriage.

questions.stem:
(a) Define the term urban slum.
(b) Using examples from cities in West Africa, describe any four factors that have contributed to the development of urban slums.
(c) State four ways in which a government can reduce urban slums.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) An urban slum is an overcrowded, densely built-up part of a city with poor-quality, often illegal housing, lacking basic amenities (water, sanitation, drainage, electricity), occupied mainly by low-income people
3 marks: (b) Rapid rural-urban migration into cities such as Lagos (Ajegunle, Makoko), Accra (Nima) and Dakar
3 marks: (b) Poverty/low incomes and high cost of housing and land, forcing people into cheap, crowded dwellings
3 marks: (b) Poor planning and weak enforcement of building regulations
3 marks: (b) Inadequate provision of social amenities and infrastructure, and growth of old city cores (e.g. Ibadan's core, Kano old city)
1 mark: (c) Slum clearance and redevelopment/urban renewal
1 mark: (c) Provision of low-cost housing
1 mark: (c) Provision of amenities (water, roads, drainage, electricity) and enforcement of planning laws
1 mark: (c) Rural development to check rural-urban migration
questions.explanation: (a) An urban slum is a densely populated, run-down area of a city with overcrowded, poorly built and often unauthorised houses, lacking basic amenities such as water, sanitation, drainage and electricity, and inhabited mostly by the poor. (b) Slums in West African cities have developed because of rapid rural-urban migration, as people flock to Lagos (Ajegunle, Makoko), Accra (Nima) and Abidjan in search of jobs; because of poverty and the high cost of land and rent, which force migrants into cheap, crowded dwellings; because of poor town planning and weak enforcement of building regulations; and because amenities and infrastructure have not kept pace with growth, while the old indigenous cores of cities such as Ibadan and Kano have decayed. (c) Governments can reduce slums through slum clearance and urban renewal, building low-cost housing estates, providing amenities and enforcing planning laws, and developing rural areas to reduce migration.

questions.stem:
(a) Write notes on any two classes of water transport.
(b) With reference to Nigeria, explain the advantages that will be derived from the improvement of a named water transport.
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Inland waterways: transport on rivers, lakes and canals (e.g. Niger and Benue rivers, Lagos lagoon) using canoes, barges and steamers; cheap for bulky goods but affected by seasonal water levels, rapids and silting
3 marks: (a) Ocean/sea transport: carries passengers and goods between countries by ships along ocean routes; cheapest for bulky, heavy international cargo; requires ports and harbours
2 marks: (a) Further details on chosen classes, e.g. coastal shipping between ports of the same country, ferries
2 marks: (b) Named water transport, e.g. inland waterway on the River Niger/Benue
2 marks: (b) Cheap movement of bulky goods (grains, cement, petroleum products, livestock) between the north and south
2 marks: (b) Reduces pressure and damage on roads and road accidents
2 marks: (b) Creates employment and stimulates trade, fishing and growth of river ports (e.g. Lokoja, Onitsha, Baro)
2 marks: (b) Opens up remote riverine areas and links with neighbouring countries (Niger, Cameroon)
2 marks: (b) Encourages tourism and generates revenue for government
questions.explanation: (a) Inland water transport uses rivers, lakes, lagoons and canals; in Nigeria canoes, barges and small steamers ply the Niger, Benue and Lagos lagoon. It is cheap and suitable for bulky goods but is affected by seasonal changes in water level, rapids, silting and water weeds. Ocean (sea) transport moves goods and passengers across seas and oceans in ships between ports; it is the cheapest means of carrying heavy, bulky cargo over long distances and handles most international trade, but needs ports with deep water and handling facilities. (b) Improving inland waterways on the Niger and Benue by dredging and building river ports would provide cheap transport for bulky goods such as grains, cement, fertiliser and petroleum products between the north and the coast; reduce traffic, damage and accidents on the roads; create jobs and stimulate trade, fishing and growth of river ports such as Lokoja, Onitsha and Baro; open up isolated riverine communities and link Nigeria with Niger and Cameroon; and promote tourism and government revenue.

1 mark: (c) Enugu: coal
1 mark: (c) Jos: tin (and columbite)
1 mark: (c) Makurdi: yams/beniseed (soya beans)
1 mark: (c) Kaduna: textiles/cotton (petroleum products from the refinery)

questions.explanation: (c) Enugu is noted for coal, Jos for tin and columbite, Makurdi for yams and beniseed, Kaduna for textiles (cotton) and petroleum products, and Ibadan for cocoa. (d) Nigeria's railways suffer from old, narrow-gauge, mostly single-track lines and obsolete locomotives and wagons that are poorly maintained, so trains are slow and breakdowns and derailments are frequent. They also suffer from poor management, corruption and inadequate funding, and from strong competition from more flexible road transport, which has led to low patronage and heavy losses.

questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) Transhumance: seasonal movement of herdsmen (mainly Fulani) and their cattle in search of pasture and water - southwards to the river valleys and Middle Belt in the dry season, back north in the rainy season to escape tsetse flies
4 marks: (a)(ii)/(iii) Intensive farming: high inputs of labour/capital on small land near towns, with manure/fertiliser, irrigation and continuous cropping (e.g. Kano close-settled zone, market gardening). Terrace farming: step-like platforms cut on hillsides to check erosion and conserve water, e.g. Jos Plateau, Obudu, Mandara/Biu areas
2 marks: (c) Pests and diseases such as trypanosomiasis spread by tsetse flies, rinderpest
2 marks: (c) Shortage of pasture and water in the dry season; poor breeds with low yields
2 marks: (c) Lack of capital, veterinary services and storage/processing facilities; conflict with crop farmers
questions.explanation: (a) Transhumance is the seasonal migration of pastoralists, mainly the Fulani, with their cattle in search of pasture and water: in the dry season they move south to the river valleys and Middle Belt, and in the rainy season they return north to avoid tsetse flies and use fresh pasture. Intensive farming involves using much labour and capital on small plots, applying manure or fertilisers, irrigating and cropping continuously to obtain high yields, as in the close-settled zone around Kano and market gardens near cities. questions.stem:
Compare the Cross River Basin with the Sokoto Plains under the following headings:
(a) Climate
(b) Resources
(c) Problems of development.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Cross River Basin: tropical wet/rain forest climate with heavy rainfall (over 2,000 mm) and a long rainy season (8-10 months)
2 marks: (a) Sokoto Plains: tropical continental/Sahel-Sudan climate with low rainfall (under 750 mm), short rainy season (3-4 months) and long dry season with harmattan
2 marks: (a) Cross River: high humidity and small temperature range; Sokoto: low humidity, very high temperatures and large daily/annual range
2 marks: (b) Cross River: rain forest timber, oil palm, cocoa, rubber; fish; limestone (cement at Calabar), and tourism (Obudu)
2 marks: (b) Sokoto: livestock (cattle, goats - hides and skins), millet, guinea corn, groundnuts, onions; limestone/phosphates (cement at Sokoto)
2 marks: (b) Sokoto: fadama land/irrigation along Sokoto-Rima rivers (rice, wheat); Cross River: Cross River for transport and fishing
2 marks: (c) Cross River: dense forest and swampy, hilly terrain make road building difficult; heavy rainfall causes erosion and flooding
2 marks: (c) Cross River: leaching of soils, tsetse/disease, isolation of some areas
2 marks: (c) Sokoto: drought, desert encroachment and water shortage; poor soils
2 marks: (c) Sokoto: remoteness from the coast/ports, low industrial development, illiteracy and herders-farmers conflict
questions.explanation: (a) The Cross River Basin in south-eastern Nigeria has a hot, wet equatorial/tropical rain forest climate with heavy rainfall of over 2,000 mm spread over eight to ten months, high humidity and a small temperature range. The Sokoto Plains in the extreme north-west have a tropical continental (Sudan-Sahel) climate with low rainfall under about 750 mm in three to four months, a long dry season with harmattan, very high temperatures and a large range. (b) The Cross River Basin has rain forest timber, oil palm, cocoa and rubber, fishing in the river and estuary, limestone for the Calabar cement works and tourist attractions such as Obudu. The Sokoto Plains are rich in livestock (cattle, goats, sheep, hides and skins), grains such as millet and guinea corn, groundnuts and onions, fadama lands along the Sokoto-Rima for irrigated rice and wheat, and limestone and phosphates for the Sokoto cement works. (c) In the Cross River Basin, dense forest, swamps and hilly terrain hinder road construction, heavy rains cause leaching, erosion and floods, and some areas remain isolated. In the Sokoto Plains, drought, desert encroachment and water shortage, poor sandy soils, remoteness from the ports and low industrialisation hamper development.

questions.stem:
Explain how the following factors affect rainfall distribution in Africa:
(a) Ocean currents
(b) Distance from the sea
(c) Winds.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Warm ocean currents warm the overlying air, increasing evaporation and humidity, so onshore winds bring heavy rainfall
2 marks: (a) Example: warm Mozambique/Agulhas current gives heavy rainfall on the east coast of South Africa and Madagascar
2 marks: (a) Cold currents cool the overlying air, reducing evaporation and causing stable conditions, fog and little rain
1 mark: (a) Example: cold Benguela current helps form the Namib desert; cold Canary current the coastal Sahara
2 marks: (b) Coastal areas receive more rain because moist sea winds drop their moisture first
2 marks: (b) Rainfall decreases inland as winds lose moisture, e.g. from over 2,000 mm on the Nigerian coast to below 500 mm in the far north
1 mark: (b) Interior regions far from the sea, e.g. the Sahara, Kalahari, are dry
2 marks: (c) Onshore moist winds bring rain, e.g. the south-west monsoon (tropical maritime air) brings rain to West Africa
2 marks: (c) Offshore/dry continental winds bring little rain, e.g. the north-east trades (harmattan) cause the dry season
2 marks: (c) Seasonal shifting of wind belts and the ITCZ/convergence of winds produces seasonal rainfall; winds forced over highlands give relief rain on windward slopes (e.g. Cameroon Mountain) and rain shadow on leeward sides
2 marks: (c) Westerlies bring winter rain to the Mediterranean coasts of North Africa and the Cape region
questions.explanation: (a) Warm ocean currents, such as the Mozambique and Agulhas currents off south-east Africa, warm the air above them, increasing evaporation and moisture, so onshore winds crossing them bring heavy rain to the adjacent coasts. Cold currents, such as the Benguela off south-west Africa and the Canary off north-west Africa, chill the air, making it stable and producing fog but little rain, which contributes to the coastal Namib and Sahara deserts. (b) Places near the sea receive the moist onshore winds first and get the most rainfall; as the winds move inland they lose moisture, so rainfall decreases with distance from the coast, as in Nigeria from over 2,000 mm at the coast to below 500 mm in the north-east, and the far interiors such as the Sahara and Kalahari are arid. (c) Moist onshore winds, like the south-west monsoon in West Africa, bring rain, while dry continental winds such as the north-east trades (harmattan) cause the dry season; the seasonal movement of the ITCZ shifts these wind belts north and south, giving seasonal rainfall; winds forced up highlands like the Cameroon Mountain give heavy relief rain on windward slopes and rain shadow on leeward sides; and the westerlies bring winter rain to the Mediterranean north and Cape south.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe any four ways in which lines of longitude are different from lines of latitude.
(b) Calculate the approximate distance in a straight line between Tema (Latitude 6 degrees N) and London (Latitude 52 degrees N). (Show all workings clearly).
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Longitudes (meridians) run north-south from pole to pole; latitudes (parallels) run east-west round the earth
2 marks: (a) Lines of longitude are all equal in length (semi-circles); lines of latitude decrease in length from the equator to the poles
2 marks: (a) Longitudes converge/meet at the poles; latitudes are parallel and never meet
2 marks: (a) Longitude is measured east or west of the Prime (Greenwich) Meridian 0-180 degrees and is used to calculate time; latitude is measured north or south of the equator 0-90 degrees and relates to climate zones
2 marks: (b) Tema and London lie on (approximately) the same meridian (0 degrees), both north of the equator, so subtract: 52 - 6 = 46 degrees
2 marks: (b) One degree of latitude is approximately 111 km (69 miles)
2 marks: (b) Distance = 46 x 111 km
2 marks: (b) = approximately 5,106 km (about 3,174 miles)
questions.explanation: (a) Lines of longitude run from pole to pole in a north-south direction, while lines of latitude run east-west around the globe. All meridians are equal half great circles, whereas parallels get shorter from the equator (a great circle) to the poles, where they become points. Meridians converge at the poles while parallels never meet. Longitude is measured from 0 to 180 degrees east or west of the Greenwich Meridian and is used to determine local time (15 degrees = 1 hour), while latitude is measured from 0 to 90 degrees north or south of the equator and helps to describe climatic zones. (b) Tema and London are roughly on the same meridian and both in the northern hemisphere, so the difference in latitude is 52 - 6 = 46 degrees. Since 1 degree of latitude is about 111 km, the distance is 46 x 111 = about 5,106 km (or 46 x 69 = about 3,174 miles).

(b) Outline four major differences between sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.

2 marks: (a) Metamorphic: e.g. marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss, schist (any two)
3 marks: (b) Sedimentary rocks are formed from deposition and compaction of sediments; metamorphic rocks form from alteration of existing rocks by great heat and/or pressure
3 marks: (b) Sedimentary rocks are stratified (in layers); metamorphic rocks are often foliated/banded or crystalline but not bedded
3 marks: (b) Sedimentary rocks may contain fossils; metamorphic rocks rarely contain fossils since they are destroyed
3 marks: (b) Sedimentary rocks are generally soft, porous and easily eroded; metamorphic rocks are hard, compact and resistant
questions.explanation: (a) Sedimentary rocks: sandstone and limestone (also shale, coal). Metamorphic rocks: marble and slate (also quartzite, gneiss). (b) Sedimentary rocks are formed by the deposition, compaction and cementation of sediments or organic remains, while metamorphic rocks are formed when existing igneous or sedimentary rocks are changed by intense heat and pressure. Sedimentary rocks occur in strata or layers, whereas metamorphic rocks are crystalline and often foliated or banded. Sedimentary rocks frequently contain fossils, while metamorphic rocks seldom do because the heat and pressure destroy them. Sedimentary rocks are usually soft, porous and easily weathered, whereas metamorphic rocks are harder, more compact and resistant to erosion.

questions.stem:
(a)(i) Name two landforms produced by faulting.
(ii) Describe the characteristic features of one of the landforms named in (a)(i) above.
(b) Highlight the importance of mountains to man.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Rift valley and block mountain/horst (also fault scarp/escarpment)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Rift valley: a long, narrow, flat-floored depression formed when a block of land sinks between two parallel faults
2 marks: (a)(ii) It is bounded by steep walls/fault scarps on both sides
2 marks: (a)(ii) It is often occupied by long, narrow, deep lakes or rivers and may have volcanoes nearby; e.g. East African Rift Valley, Rhine Rift Valley
2 marks: (b) Mountains attract rainfall (relief rain) and are sources of rivers for water supply and HEP
2 marks: (b) They contain minerals and forests for timber
2 marks: (b) They are tourist attractions/resorts and have cool climates for highland agriculture (e.g. tea, Irish potatoes) and grazing
2 marks: (b) They serve as natural boundaries and offered defence/protection
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Faulting produces rift valleys, block mountains (horsts) and fault scarps. (ii) A rift valley is a long, narrow trough formed when the land between two roughly parallel normal faults sinks, or when the sides are pushed up by compression. It has a flat floor and steep, straight walls (fault scarps), is often very long, as in the East African Rift Valley, and commonly contains long, deep lakes such as Lake Tanganyika, rivers and volcanoes. (b) Mountains cause relief rainfall and are sources of rivers that provide water and hydro-electric power; they contain minerals and forests; their cool climate supports highland farming and grazing, and their scenery attracts tourists; they also act as natural boundaries and have historically provided defence.

questions.stem:
(a) With the aid of a well-labelled diagram, describe a typical soil profile.
(b) Highlight the importance of soil.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) A soil profile is a vertical section of the soil from the surface to the bedrock showing distinct layers (horizons)
2 marks: (a) O horizon/litter: top layer of fresh and decaying leaves and organic matter
2 marks: (a) A horizon (topsoil): dark, rich in humus and living organisms, zone of eluviation/leaching
2 marks: (a) B horizon (subsoil): zone of illuviation where leached minerals (iron, clay) accumulate; lighter, compact
2 marks: (a) C horizon: weathered parent material; D/R horizon: unweathered bedrock
2 marks: (b) Soil supports plant growth and agriculture, providing food for man and animals
2 marks: (b) It is a habitat for organisms and stores water and minerals
2 marks: (b) It provides raw materials (clay for pottery, bricks, building), supports foundations and is used for construction/road building
questions.explanation: (a) A soil profile is a vertical section through the soil from the surface down to the bedrock, showing horizons. At the top is a layer of leaf litter and organic matter (O horizon). Below it the A horizon, or topsoil, is dark, crumbly and rich in humus and soil organisms; water percolating through it leaches out soluble minerals. The B horizon, or subsoil, is lighter in colour and more compact, where leached iron, aluminium and clay accumulate (illuviation). The C horizon consists of partly weathered parent rock, resting on the unweathered bedrock (R horizon). A diagram would show these layers labelled from top to bottom. (b) Soil is the medium for plant growth and therefore the basis of agriculture and food supply; it stores water and nutrients and is the habitat of many organisms; it provides raw materials such as clay for pottery, bricks and building, and it supports buildings and roads.

(b) Describe three uses each of any two of the resources listed in (a) above.
(c) Name three other environmental resources that are of great importance to man.
questions.markingGuide:

4 marks: (b) Sunlight (any three uses): needed for photosynthesis; source of solar power/electricity; drying of crops, fish and clothes; provides vitamin D/warmth

questions.explanation: (a) Atmospheric resources include sunlight (solar energy), air (oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide), wind and rainfall (water vapour). (b) Sunlight is used by green plants for photosynthesis, can be converted into electricity with solar panels, and is used for drying crops, fish and clothes, as well as giving warmth. Wind turns turbines to generate electricity and windmills to pump water, is used in winnowing grain and for sailing boats, and helps in pollination and seed dispersal. (Rainfall provides water for agriculture, homes and industries and feeds rivers for HEP.) (c) Other important environmental resources are land (soil), water bodies such as rivers, lakes and seas, forests (vegetation), minerals and wildlife.

Study the table below and answer the questions that follow.
Month: J, F, M, A, M, J, J, A, S, O, N, D.

(a)(i) Calculate the mean annual temperature. [2 marks]

questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) Sum of monthly temperatures = 363 degrees C
1 mark: (a)(i) Mean = 363 / 12 = 30.25 degrees C

questions.explanation: (i) The monthly temperatures total 363 degrees C, so the mean annual temperature is 363 / 12 = 30.25 degrees C. (ii) The highest temperature is 35 degrees C (July) and the lowest 26 degrees C (January/February), so the annual range is 9 degrees C. (iii) Annual precipitation is only 150 mm, with no rain at all from May to September, and temperatures are high all year with the hottest months in mid-year; this is a hot (tropical) desert climate of the northern hemisphere.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between rotation and revolution of the earth. [4 marks]
(b) Describe three effects each of the earth's rotation and revolution. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Rotation is the spinning of the earth on its own axis from west to east, taking about 24 hours
2 marks: (a) Revolution is the movement of the earth in its orbit round the sun, taking about 365 1/4 days (one year)
2 marks: (b) Rotation causes day and night
2 marks: (b) Rotation causes differences in time between places (1 hour per 15 degrees of longitude)
2 marks: (b) Rotation deflects winds and ocean currents (Coriolis force/Ferrel's law); also causes daily rise and fall of tides and apparent movement of the sun
2 marks: (b) Revolution, with the inclined axis, causes the four seasons
2 marks: (b) Revolution causes variation in the length of day and night at different times of the year
2 marks: (b) Revolution causes the apparent movement of the overhead sun between the tropics (equinoxes and solstices) and the changing altitude of the midday sun; leap year
questions.explanation: (a) Rotation is the spinning of the earth on its axis from west to east, completed in about 24 hours. Revolution is the earth's movement along its elliptical orbit round the sun, completed in about 365 1/4 days. (b) Rotation causes day and night as each part of the earth turns towards and away from the sun; it causes time differences between places, 1 hour for every 15 degrees of longitude; and it deflects winds and ocean currents to the right in the northern hemisphere and left in the southern (Coriolis effect), as well as contributing to tides and the apparent daily movement of the sun. Revolution, combined with the tilt of the axis, causes the seasons; it causes variation in the length of day and night through the year; and it causes the apparent migration of the overhead sun between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, giving the equinoxes and solstices (and the need for a leap year every four years).

questions.stem: (b) Explain with examples, reasons for which the continental shelves provide the world's major fishing grounds. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Shallow water (less than about 200 m) allows sunlight to penetrate, so plankton (fish food) grows abundantly
2 marks: Rivers bring nutrients/minerals from the land that support plankton growth
2 marks: Meeting of warm and cold currents (e.g. Gulf Stream and Labrador current on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland; Kuroshio and Oyashio off Japan) brings nutrients and good conditions for plankton and fish
2 marks: The shallow, gently sloping floor provides breeding and spawning grounds and makes it easy to set nets/trawl
2 marks: Examples of fishing grounds: Grand Banks (North-West Atlantic), Dogger Bank (North Sea), North-West Pacific off Japan, Peru coast (Humboldt current)
questions.explanation: Continental shelves are the gently sloping, submerged margins of the continents, usually less than about 200 m deep. Because the water is shallow, sunlight penetrates to the bottom, allowing abundant growth of plankton, the main food of fish. Rivers draining the land bring mineral nutrients that further enrich the water. On many shelves warm and cold currents meet, such as the Gulf Stream and Labrador current over the Grand Banks of Newfoundland or the Kuroshio and Oyashio off Japan, stirring up nutrients and creating ideal conditions for plankton and fish. The shallow floor also provides spawning grounds and makes trawling and netting easy. Hence the major fishing grounds, the Grand Banks, the Dogger Bank in the North Sea, the North-West Pacific off Japan and the Peruvian coast, are on continental shelves.

questions.stem:
(a) Define mass wasting. [2 marks]
(b) List two factors affecting mass wasting. [2 marks]
(c) Describe any two types of mass wasting. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Mass wasting is the downslope movement of weathered rock materials and soil under the influence of gravity
1 mark: (b) Steepness of slope
1 mark: (b) Amount of water (rainfall) in the material; also vegetation cover, nature of rock, earthquakes, human activities
2 marks: (c) Soil creep: very slow, almost imperceptible downslope movement of soil
2 marks: (c) Soil creep is caused by alternate wetting and drying, freezing and thawing, and gravity; evidence includes tilted trees, poles and fences and terracettes
2 marks: (c) Landslide: sudden, rapid movement of large masses of rock and soil down a steep slope
2 marks: (c) Landslides are triggered by heavy rain lubricating the material, earthquakes or undercutting of slopes; they leave scars and debris at the foot
2 marks: (c) (or) Mudflow/earthflow: rapid flow of water-saturated fine material down a slope or valley; (or) rockfall, slump
2 marks: (c) Effects/examples of the chosen types, e.g. destruction of roads, houses and farmland
questions.explanation: (a) Mass wasting (mass movement) is the movement of weathered rock and soil down a slope under the pull of gravity. (b) It is influenced by the steepness of the slope and by the amount of water in the material, as well as by vegetation cover, rock type, earthquakes and human activities. (c) Soil creep is the very slow, almost imperceptible movement of soil downslope, caused by alternate wetting and drying or freezing and thawing combined with gravity; it is shown by tilted trees, poles and fences, bent walls and small terraces (terracettes) on slopes. A landslide is the sudden, rapid sliding of large masses of rock and soil down a steep slope, often triggered by heavy rain that lubricates the material, by earthquakes or by undercutting of the slope by rivers, waves or road construction; it leaves a bare scar above and a heap of debris below and can bury roads, houses and farmland. (Mudflows, rapid flows of water-saturated fine material, are another type.)

questions.stem:
Write explanatory notes on any two of the following:
(a) convectional rainfall; [8 marks]
(b) land and sea breezes; [8 marks]
(c) Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Convectional rainfall: intense heating of the ground causes air to warm, expand and rise in convection currents
2 marks: (a) The rising air cools adiabatically to dew point; condensation forms towering cumulonimbus clouds
2 marks: (a) Heavy downpours, often with thunder and lightning, usually in the afternoon
2 marks: (a) Common in equatorial regions and in the tropics during the rainy season
2 marks: (b) Land and sea breezes result from differential heating of land and sea
2 marks: (b) Sea breeze: by day land heats faster, low pressure forms over land, cool air blows from sea to land
2 marks: (b) Land breeze: at night land cools faster, high pressure over land, air blows from land to sea
2 marks: (b) They moderate coastal temperatures and are used by fishermen (go out with land breeze, return with sea breeze)
questions.explanation: (a) Convectional rainfall occurs when the ground is strongly heated by the sun, so the air above it warms, expands and rises in convection currents. As it rises it cools adiabatically until it reaches dew point; the water vapour condenses to form tall cumulonimbus clouds, which give heavy showers, often with thunder and lightning, usually in the afternoon or evening. It is typical of equatorial regions throughout the year and of the tropics in the rainy season. (b) Land and sea breezes are local winds caused by the unequal heating of land and sea. By day the land heats faster than the sea, so the air over it rises, creating low pressure, and cooler air flows in from the sea as a sea breeze. At night the land cools faster, pressure becomes higher over the land, and air flows out to sea as a land breeze. They moderate coastal temperatures and help fishermen, who sail out with the land breeze and return with the sea breeze. (The ITCZ is the low-pressure belt where the north-east and south-east trades converge; it moves north and south with the overhead sun, bringing rainy and dry seasons to West Africa.)

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four conditions that favour the formation of delta. [8 marks]
(b) Describe any two types of delta. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The river must carry a large load of sediment (from active erosion in its upper course)
2 marks: (a) The sea or lake at the mouth should be shallow and calm, with weak tides and currents that cannot remove the sediment
2 marks: (a) The river should flow slowly in its lower course so that deposition occurs; the meeting with salt water causes flocculation of clay particles
2 marks: (a) The coast should be stable (no subsidence) and there should be no large lake upstream to trap sediment
2 marks: (b) Arcuate (fan-shaped) delta: triangular/fan shape with a convex seaward edge and many distributaries, composed of coarse material, e.g. Niger delta, Nile delta
2 marks: (b) Arcuate delta features: lagoons, swamps and sand bars along the front
2 marks: (b) Bird's foot delta: long, finger-like distributaries extending into the sea, bordered by levees, made of fine material, e.g. Mississippi delta
2 marks: (b) (or) Estuarine/cuspate delta: formed in a submerged river mouth or shaped like a tooth by waves, e.g. Seine, Tiber
questions.explanation: (a) Deltas form where a river carries a large load of sediment eroded from its basin; where the sea or lake at the mouth is shallow and fairly calm, with weak tides and currents that cannot carry the deposits away; where the river slows on entering the sea and the salt water causes fine clay particles to flocculate and settle; and where the coast is stable and no lake upstream traps the sediment. (b) An arcuate (fan-shaped) delta, like those of the Niger and the Nile, is roughly triangular with a curved seaward edge; it is made of fairly coarse sediment and crossed by many distributaries, with swamps, lagoons and sand bars. A bird's-foot delta, like that of the Mississippi, has long, finger-like distributaries extending far into the sea, each bordered by levees of fine silt, giving the shape of a bird's foot. (An estuarine delta forms within a drowned river mouth, and a cuspate delta is shaped like a tooth by wave action.)

questions.stem:
(a) Define environmental balance. [2 marks]
(b) With the aid of a diagram, explain the water cycle. [8 marks]
(c) In what three ways is water cycle important to man? [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Environmental balance is the state of equilibrium/stability among the living and non-living components of the environment, where natural processes and resources are maintained without degradation
2 marks: (b) Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, rivers and soil, and plants release water by transpiration (evapotranspiration)
2 marks: (b) Water vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds; winds carry the clouds over land
2 marks: (b) Water returns to the earth as precipitation (rain, snow, hail)
2 marks: (b) It flows over the surface as run-off into rivers or infiltrates as groundwater, eventually returning to the sea, and the cycle repeats (a labelled diagram shows these stages)
2 marks: (c) It provides rainfall for agriculture and fresh water for domestic and industrial use
2 marks: (c) It feeds rivers and lakes used for hydro-electric power, transport and fishing
2 marks: (c) It helps to regulate climate/temperature and recycles and purifies water, supporting all life
questions.explanation: (a) Environmental balance is the condition in which the living organisms and the physical components of the environment interact in a stable equilibrium, so that natural cycles continue and resources are not degraded. (b) The water cycle is the continuous circulation of water between the earth and the atmosphere. Heat from the sun evaporates water from seas, lakes, rivers and moist soil, and plants give off water vapour through transpiration. The vapour rises, cools and condenses around dust particles to form clouds, which winds carry over the land. When the droplets become large they fall as precipitation, rain, snow or hail. Some of the water runs off the surface into streams and rivers, some infiltrates the soil to become groundwater, and some is taken up by plants; eventually it flows back to the sea, where the cycle begins again. A diagram shows the sea, evaporation arrows, clouds, rain over hills, run-off, infiltration and rivers returning to the sea. (c) The water cycle supplies rainfall for farming and fresh water for homes and industries; it keeps rivers and lakes flowing for hydro-electric power, transport and fishing; and it regulates climate and continually renews and purifies the earth's water.
